IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01122

The challenge of interpreting sacred texts is comparable in the two traditions, and they speak of the same ancient prophets. A future comparative spiritual interpretation of scripture should therefore be more than an attempt to reconstruct past theology. It should become a new event in its own right: the discovery of the shared pattern of spiritual experience that belongs to the encounter with a Holy Book, a pattern already suggested by the great spiritual commentaries on the Bible and the Qur'an.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01123

In either tradition, the subject of spiritual interpretation cannot be held at a cold, neutral distance. The interpreter and the reality being interpreted become involved in one another. That is why a true meeting between interpreters from the two traditions can happen only in the time of the soul.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01124

The calling of those who possess inner knowledge (orafa) and those who pursue divine wisdom (hokama) stands beyond every earthly social or political order. They can do only one thing: invite each person to undergo a transformation, to give birth to and nurture their own “subtle body of resurrection.” This calling does not depend on belonging to a religious institution; it draws people out of the ordinary bonds of social belonging.
IV. The Phenomenon of the Sacred Book
passage-en-01125

Yet it also brings into being people in whom Heaven and Earth meet invisibly. In that meeting lie the Mafatih al-Ghayb, the keys to the hidden world. These, and these alone, are the “keys of the Kingdom.” If we lose sight of that, we will never understand how those who possessed these keys were able to use them.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01126
Chapter V The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
en-book-1-ch-5-s1
1. The Secret of the Imams, or the Four Levels of Inner Meaning
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01127

Everything we have seen so far points to a central idea: at its heart, Shiism understands itself as the inner meaning (batin) of the revelation brought by the Prophet. In this sense, it is the inner, hidden dimension of Islam. The idea that drives this understanding is walayat, the spiritual bond and authority of the Imams. It is itself defined as “the inner, hidden meaning of the prophetic message” (batin al-nubuwwat).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01128

What we began to explore in Chapter II—the meaning of prophecy, the cycles through which revelation unfolds, the knowledge inherited from the prophets, and the place of the Imam in Shiite spiritual life—all centres on walayat. And that brings us back to the sacred Book. The Imam is not only the “guardian who upholds the Qur'an” (Qa'im bi'l-Qur'an). The very idea of the Imam, and of the spiritual role passed from Imam to Imam, lies at the heart of how the Qur'an's inner meaning is discovered.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01129

To understand this, we must look at the Shiite idea of the Imam on the spiritual and metaphysical level where it first takes shape. It is fundamentally different from the Sunni idea, in which the imam is the head of the community and the centre of its social order, responsible for such matters as government, justice, and the army.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01130

However demanding the moral standards placed on such a leader may be, they concern the outward sphere of life (zahir). Sunni thought, in this account, does not require a metaphysical doctrine of the Imam, nor does it require the Imam to possess the divinely given freedom from error and impurity (isma) which Shiism attributes to the Fourteen Pure Ones and finds expressly affirmed in certain verses of the Qur'an. Shiism, by contrast, understands the Imam primarily through the inner dimension (batin).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01131

Because the Imam fulfils a spiritual role that reaches beyond the visible world, the very nature of his person must be understood in that light. Twelver Shiites, in the thousands of reports and sayings (hadiths) they study and interpret, are not drawing up a political programme for the Imamate. This is not a contest between rival political factions, like the medieval Guelphs and Ghibellines.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01132

An Imam does not need to exercise any earthly power to be the Imam—the hidden spiritual centre of the world. Twelver Shiites know perfectly well that the world, as it is now, cannot know or recognise him.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01133

Indeed, since there can be only twelve Imams, the disappearance from public sight of the Twelfth Imam—his occultation (ghayba)—is not an accident of history. It follows from the very structure of the Imamate. Among others, Mulla Sadra Shirazi has set out, in a few exceptionally dense pages, the differences between the Sunni and Shiite understandings of the Imam.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01134

To grasp who the Imam is, and what he does, within Shiite thought, we must take in the whole range of what we earlier called the “octaves of universes”: the many levels of reality through which spiritual interpretation rises. We have already encountered a saying of the Fifth Imam (above, p. 99) which immediately places the whole of this “philosophy of prophecy” against the background of the first creation: the complete company, or pleroma, of fourteen beings of light, sometimes called the Fourteen Aeons.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01135

At each level we encounter a deeper meaning, an inner reality. Without it, the outward story of events in the world we see and touch would belong to a dead past and have no meaning beyond it. That is why the same Imam warned us, in effect, against reducing revelation to past history. The sacred Book remains alive forever because its inner meaning continues to unfold in every faithful believer.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01136

The spiritual meaning of the Imams and the interpretation of scripture follow the same movement, both upward and downward through the levels of reality. They are inseparable parts of a single process unfolding from world to world. The complete company of the Fourteen Pure Ones (Chaharde Ma'sum) appears, as a manifestation of God, at every level of this great order.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01137

The prophetic Word, or Logos, is revealed from level to level, from one station to another, always together with the Light that reveals its secret, inner meaning. The “eternal Qur'an” likewise descends through the worlds. It changes in form as it moves from the original, archetypal Book, existing as pure intelligible reality, to the material book we hold in our world—a book that still carries the secrets of every world through which it has descended.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01138

The Imamate accompanies this descent of the prophetic Word and the Book through all its stations or dwelling places (maqamat). To know those worlds is the purpose of hikmat ilahiya, divine wisdom. Such knowledge is what we mean here by spiritual knowledge, or gnosis, because to know these worlds is to be born anew, to rise back through them, and to return to them.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01139

The Arabic word for spiritual interpretation, ta'wil, means precisely “to lead something back to its origin, its original pattern” (asl). The Imam guides us on that return. And this brings us back to a saying we have already quoted (above, p. 116), one of those brief sayings in which the Imams express the very heart of Shiism.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01140

The saying is exceptionally difficult, and its allusions need a little explanation. It provides, as it were, the key to interpreting hidden meanings. It comes to us through Saffar Qummi (died 290 AH / 903 CE), a disciple of the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari, who included it in his great collection of traditions. These traditions are a basic source for understanding the spiritual nature of the Imams. In fact, we have two sayings, or two versions of a single saying, in which the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, expresses the same thought.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01141
We will call them versions A and B.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01142

Version A: “Our cause (amruna, res nostra) is truth (haqq), and the truth of truth. It is the outward meaning, and the inner meaning of the outward, and the inner meaning of the inner. It is the secret (sirr), and the secret of the secret (sirr al-sirr); it is the secret of what remains concealed (sirr al-mustasirr), a secret still wrapped in secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01143
Version B: “Our cause is a secret that remains concealed (sirr mustasirr), a secret that only a secret can teach, a secret upon a secret (sirr 'ala sirr), a secret still wrapped in secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01144

Both versions speak in the same compressed, suggestive language, though they differ slightly from the wording quoted earlier. In this form, the two versions appear in a large commentary by Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i (died 1241 AH / 1826 CE) on a classic text of Twelver Shiite devotion: The Comprehensive Spiritual Visitation of the Twelve Imams (al-Ziyarat al-jami'a). That work is a long series of greetings to the Imams. It names their spiritual and metaphysical qualities with great precision, making it particularly useful for understanding the different levels of reality to which the Imams belong—and, at the same time, the different levels on which the Qur'an can be understood.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01145

The two versions of Ja'far's saying appear near the start of Ahsa'i's commentary, where he explains the greeting: “Peace be upon you, members of the Prophet's Family, who are the place where the prophetic message is received” (mawda' al-risala).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01146

Ahsa'i arranges the levels described in the sayings into four maqams, placing them in order from the highest level of reality to the lowest. For convenience, we will keep the Arabic word maqam (plural maqamat), which can mean a position, station, rank, dwelling place, or level. In music it can also mean a mode or melodic pattern; twelve such modes are traditionally counted.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01147
The first maqam is mentioned fourth in both versions. It is “the secret still wrapped in secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01148
The second maqam is called “the secret of the secret” in version A and “a secret upon a secret” in version B. Version A also calls it “the inner meaning of the inner” (batin al-batin).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01149
The first and second maqams together are what version A calls “the truth of truth” (haqq al-haqq).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01150
The third maqam is simply “the secret” (al-sirr) in version A, as well as “the inner meaning of the outward” (batin al-zahir). Version B calls it “a secret that only a secret can teach.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01151

The fourth maqam is called “the outward meaning” in version A. Version B places it first and calls it “a secret that remains concealed” (sirr mustasirr). The third and fourth maqams together are what version A calls simply “truth” (al-haqq).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01152
What, then, makes this fourfold order possible? What understanding of reality lies behind it? Here again, we will follow Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i as closely as we can.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01153

1. The first maqam is the level of what has never been revealed. It is the dwelling place of “the secret still wrapped in secret”: the unfathomable depth of primordial Oneness, the Truth of Truth, the Reality that makes reality itself possible—the source that brings existence into being. Within this mystery the command to be is given eternally: the divine “Be!” (esto). Without it, there could be no act of existing (wujud), nothing that exists (mawjud), and nothing with a distinct nature or essence (mahiyya).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01154

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i explains this through a comparison. Think of a man called Zayd, who is standing. What is the relationship between Zayd and the act of standing (qiyam)? When we say “Zayd is standing” (qa'im), we describe Zayd as he appears in that position. We see standing made visible in the person of Zayd.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01155

But “Zayd standing” is neither Zayd himself, considered apart from his actions, nor the act of standing considered on its own. Zayd stands because of the act of standing; yet what we actually see is a man standing, not “standing” itself.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01156

We can perceive the act only through someone who is standing. In a sense, standing is invisibly present in the standing man. It is revealed through him, although it is also what makes him stand. The act becomes visible only through the man, and the man possesses the quality of standing only through the act that makes a standing person possible (wujud qa'im). The same is true when Zayd sits, speaks, or performs any other action.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01157

We can point to these conditions and activities in him, and we know him through them, but they are not Zayd himself. They resemble him in the sense that they are ways in which we encounter and recognise him.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01158
Yet no single quality is identical with his own essence (dhat), with Zayd as a person. We therefore say that these qualities come from Zayd without being Zayd himself.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01159

This comparison helps us understand the level of reality occupied by the Imams in their original, complete existence as beings of light. It also helps us move from the first maqam to the second: the eternal emergence of the “primordial Muhammadan Reality” (Haqiqat Muhammadiya) within what remains forever unrevealed. A prayer for the month of Rajab, traditionally attributed to the Twelfth Imam, addresses God in these words:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01160

You have made them [the Twelve Imams] the original dwelling place of Your Words (kalimat), the pillars of Your oneness (tawhid), and the signs of Your stations (maqamat)—the levels or dwelling places of Your manifestation—which are absent nowhere. Through these stations, that is, through the Imams, whoever knows You comes to know You. There is no difference between them and You, except that they are Your servants and Your creatures. Their origin is in You, and to You they return.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01161

Now the comparison becomes clearer. The underlying reality (haqiqa) of the Imams corresponds to the act of standing in the example of Zayd. That reality appears through them, just as standing becomes visible and knowable only through a person who stands. The standing person is the station (maqam) in which someone can know Zayd: the only point at which Zayd becomes known, while what he is in himself remains hidden beneath the qualities he displays.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01162

The claim that God can be known only through certain stations is meant in the same way. These stations become real through the persons of the Twelve Imams—or, more fully, through the Fourteen Pure Ones. This is the meaning of the First Imam's words: “We are the A'raf” (see Chapter VII below); “God can be known only through knowing us.” Divine reality becomes knowable only by knowing the Fourteen Pure Ones, who are the places where God becomes manifest.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01163

What we see is a person standing; we never see the act of standing on its own. We see it only through someone who stands, even though it is what allows that person to stand. Likewise, what remains unrevealed—the hidden divine reality, the Absconditum—is beyond our reach. It can be known only through its manifestations, while those manifestations themselves exist only through it. They “are Him without being Him.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01164
“There is no difference between them and You, except that they are Your servants and Your creatures.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01165

The first maqam, then, concerns the very ground of the divine essence (Kunh al-Dhat), comparable to what Meister Eckhart calls the Urgrund, the deepest ground of being. At this level we can speak of God only by saying what God is not. This is the way of negative, or apophatic, theology (tanzih).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01166

The comparison between a standing person and the act of standing is especially revealing here. What lies beneath it is the mystery of how existence first appears at all. Following the teaching of their Imams, the Shiite thinkers we are studying explored this mystery at a level beyond the one reached by the Persian Neoplatonists who followed Suhrawardi—the Ishraqiyun, or philosophers of illumination and light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01167

We need at least a rough idea of this distinction if we are to understand what these Shiite thinkers mean by the existence of the Fourteen Pure Ones before the created world, and why their account of existence begins, as it were, one level higher than that of the Illuminationists.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01168

We spoke earlier of existence being brought forth by a command: “Be!” This first calling of existence into being comes before every form that existence can take. Without it, the act of standing (qiyam) could never appear through a person who stands (qa'im), and so could never become something we know.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01169

The Arabic imperative of the verb “to be” is represented by two consonants, KN (kun: “Be!”). Above all, this idea recalls the Qur'anic verse (17:87, as cited here) in which the Prophet is told: “They ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit comes from the command of my Lord” (min amr rabbi).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01170

Yet the philosophers influenced by Neoplatonism and the thinkers who follow the Imams more strictly understand this divine command in different ways. That difference leads to two different accounts of existence itself. The Neoplatonic thinkers sometimes read the verse as saying, “The Spirit is the command of my Lord.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01171

On that reading, the Spirit creates without itself having been created. It brings existence into being and is itself, as divine command, eternally in existence. Thinkers such as Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, however, follow the Sixth Imam in teaching that the Spirit—the Holy Spirit—is the highest of created beings. They therefore distinguish two aspects of the command (amr).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01172

The first is the active command, the divine act of making something exist (amr fi'li). This act is beyond existence, and eternally comes before everything that already exists, since whatever exists, whether we speak of existence itself (wujud) or of an existing thing (mawjud), has been brought into being.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01173
The second is the command as brought into effect (amr maf'ul), the result of that act within the first created being. Here existence is considered as what the act produces.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01174

We can compare the difference to writing: the marks on the page are the result of my act of writing, although the making of the marks and the marks made belong together. Even ordinary words such as “writing” and “reading” can refer both to an action and to what that action produces or makes possible.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01175

What we are seeing here is a determined effort to understand existence at the very instant it comes into being. The Shiite thinkers call the command as brought into effect the “Light of Lights” (Nur al-Anwar), the primordial Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya), or the complete company of the Fourteen Pure Ones.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01176

On their account, the Light of Lights is the first reality to flow from the divine command: it is what comes into being through the command's action. The act that brings it forth—the active command—remains hidden in the mystery of the first maqam, “the secret still wrapped in secret.” The Light of Lights itself belongs only to the second maqam.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01177
Yet because these are two aspects of the same command, its complete transcendence and its presence within what it creates can be understood together through the Fourteen Pure Ones.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01178

Among the Neoplatonic Illuminationists, by contrast, the Light of Lights would already occupy the first maqam. It would belong to existence rather than stand beyond it. Intelligence—the Nous or 'aql—or Spirit would then be the first level of reality to flow from the Light of Lights. When the Shiite thinkers use those words, however, they mean the Intelligence or Spirit of the Muhammadan Reality itself. This Intelligence, this Spirit “which comes from the divine command,” is the Face of the primordial Muhammadan Reality.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01179

These distinctions must be sketched very briefly here, but their importance is enormous. They could clear up many misunderstandings about wahdat al-wujud, the oneness of existence, especially when it is translated too quickly as “monism,” as though everything were simply one substance. Everything depends on whether this unity begins with the Light of Lights at the first maqam or, instead, with the Light of Lights at the second.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01180
We can already glimpse how much this matters for Shiite spiritual life and for the part played in it by the Imams.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01181

The first maqam, “the secret still wrapped in secret,” is therefore the level of the active command: the original act of bringing existence into being. That is why it remains beyond our knowledge. The secret is truly hidden within the secret. At this level, tawhid, the affirmation of God's oneness, means what the Fifth Imam taught Jabir al-Ansari: “Know that nothing resembles Him” (compare Qur'an 42:9), “and worship Him without associating anything else with Him.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01182

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i explains that when we worship God, our worship is not directed towards an empty absence, a mere denial of everything we can know. God becomes present to us through the very act of worship, although in that presence God remains invisible to created beings. In the same way, the act of standing appears through the standing person, and the active command through the command that has taken effect, without the underlying reality ever becoming visible in itself.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01183

It is at the level of this manifestation—the appearing of the divine—that the ma'ani take shape. These are the positive meanings and qualities through which human beings can speak of God. The primordial Muhammadan Reality, the complete company of the Fourteen Pure Ones, the first reality called into existence, the Light of Lights: all these names refer here to what gives those divine qualities their form. As the Fifth Imam also says to Jabir:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01184

It is we [the Imams, the Fourteen Pure Ones] who are these ma'ani. We are God's Hand, His side, His tongue, His command, His decision, His knowledge, His truth. We are the Face of God turned towards the earthly world among you. Whoever recognises us has certainty as his Imam. Whoever rejects us has Sijjin [the seventh circle of the infernal world] as his Imam.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01185

“That is why,” Shaykh Ahmad says, “a person turns towards the inaccessible Essence, even though they can never reach it; and yet they never cease to find it, even as it remains forever beyond their reach.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01186

This paradox shows us where the doctrine of the Imams, together with the whole teaching about the primordial Muhammadan Reality, stands in relation to what remains unrevealed. It points to the level before existence itself is revealed—the level the Imam calls “the secret still wrapped in secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01187

The first maqam is therefore not yet the place where the prophetic message appears. Rather, it is the source of every prophetic mission, just as the active command is the source that brings its own first effect into being: the first reality to flow from it, the primordial Muhammadan Reality.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01188

2. The second maqam is the second level of divine wisdom, called “the secret of the secret.” The first maqam is the absolute Secret, forever hidden within itself: the completely concealed inner reality. The secret of that secret is the act by which the primordial divine Essence reveals itself in the very thing that conceals it. It is hidden in its manifestation and manifest in its hiddenness. This is “a secret upon a secret,” which is why the second maqam is also called “the inner meaning of the inner.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01189

Here we encounter the mystery of the first manifestation of God within the Muhammadan Reality, the complete company of the Fourteen Pure Ones. This is the level of the ma'ani: the meanings through which we understand the divine, and through which the divine makes itself known to us. They are, so to speak, our ways of understanding (modi intelligendi).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01190
In a conversation with Jabir al-Ju'fi, the Fourth Imam says:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01191

O Jabir! To fulfil tawhid is to know (ma'rifa) the God of eternal sovereignty, whom no eyes can see although He sees all eyes. He is the Subtle One, the All-Knowing, the hidden Mystery (ghayb batin), as He Himself says. As for the ma'ani, it is we [the Imams, the Fourteen Pure Ones] who are His ma'ani—the meanings of Him that are revealed to you (zahiruhu fikum). He created us from the light of His essence.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01192

Here we should recall the mystery of the heavenly Anthropos, the primordial Human Being, familiar from many traditions of spiritual knowledge. In Shiite thought, the Fourteen Pure Ones, united in their deepest being, fulfil the role of this heavenly Human Being: they are the form in which God first becomes manifest. In other words, human beings cannot speak meaningfully of God, and God cannot reveal Himself to human beings, without some form in which the divine can be understood in human terms.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01193

But this takes place “in Heaven,” in a reality beyond the senses. It does not require an incarnation in the Christian meaning of the word (see Chapter VII below). We may think here of the visionary traditions surrounding Enoch or the ascent of Isaiah.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01194

This first manifestation “in Heaven” lies at the very foundation of the Shiite understanding of the Imams. It gives that understanding a role comparable to the Christian teaching about Christ as the divine Word, or Logos. It also makes tawhid possible. Without the teaching about the Imams, a person's attempt to affirm God's oneness would risk becoming a kind of spiritual idolatry: treating an idea of God as though it were God Himself. The teaching protects us from two opposite mistakes.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01195

One is ta'til: leaving God so completely beyond our knowledge that nothing meaningful can be said of Him. The Imams prevent that by giving the ma'ani, the divine qualities and meanings, a firm place in reality. The other mistake is tashbih: treating God as though He resembled created things. The Imams prevent that too, because these qualities are not the divine Essence itself; they always point beyond themselves.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01196

Shaykh Ahmad returns to his example of Zayd. When we speak of Zayd standing or sitting, moving or resting, acting generously, or showing some other quality, we are naming different aspects of him—different meanings through which we can know him. In the same way, when the Imam says, “We are His ma'ani,” these meanings are the ways in which God, as revealed to humanity (Deus revelatus), appears to us and can be understood by us.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01197

We will return to them in Chapter VII. In relation to the divine Essence, without which they would have no reality, they are that Essence understood “in this or that way.” In relation to the concrete traces they leave behind, they are the names of personal beings who carry these qualities and make them visible. They are their forms of manifestation (mazahir).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01198

This is how we should read the many sayings that call the Fourteen Pure Ones the Attributes of God, the Names of God, the Mercy of God, the divine Face that remains when everything else has passed away, or the Face of God turned towards the world of human beings. They are the goal (maqsad) towards which anyone seeking God turns; the ways God is made known at every level of existence, and in every meaning (ma'na) through which human beings conceive of Him. They are the signs revealed “on the horizons and within souls”—in the outer world and in our inner lives (Qur'an 41:53).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01199

In short, the Fourteen Pure Ones are the original spiritual beings (arwah) who possess life within themselves and give life to others. They are the holy souls who form the “Fourteen Temples of primordial tawhid,” all sharing one and the same essence. They are the place from which the calling into existence proceeds, as well as the place from which the prophets receive their mission.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01200

An entire family of symbols points to this mystery: the letter Nun at the opening of Qur'an 68:1; the primordial Book; the “keys to the unseen” (mafatih al-ghayb); the barren Earth (compare Qur'an 33:27) and the first Water that makes it fertile; the primordial Inkwell from which the Pen—the Intelligence of the universe—draws; and the oil that is “almost ready to shine, even though no fire has touched it” (Qur'an 34:35).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01201

3. The third maqam is the level of the “thresholds” or “gates” (abwab). It is the “secret that only another secret can teach”: the inner meaning of what appears outwardly. Within the primordial Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya), this is where Intelligence—the Muhammadan Logos, the Prophet in his existence before the created world—emerges eternally.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01202

We can express this only through the images already introduced. The primordial Water falls upon barren Earth (32:27), upon a land that has no life yet (35:10). Oil bursts into flame when fire touches it (24:35). The meaning of the creative Word reaches an idea that was still lifeless, and suddenly the earth puts forth perfect growth: the lamp shines, and meaning itself comes alive. All these images lead us to the Name through which heaven and earth receive their light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01203

For the Neoplatonic Illuminationists, that Name is the Intelligence of the universe ('aql al-kull). For Shiite thinkers, it is the Pen, the Muhammadan Intelligence, the Muhammadan Spirit, or the Muhammadan Light ('aql, ruh, nur Muhammadi). These three descriptions correspond to the three forms of a saying attributed to the Prophet: “The first thing God created was my Intelligence,” or “my Spirit,” or “my Light.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01204

The Merciful One establishes Himself within this first Muhammadan Intelligence. He places within it, and brings forth from it, the unseen realities of all things: the subtle forms of creatures before they appear in the world we know. Intelligence is therefore the Gate (bab) through which God's gifts reach created beings. And because created beings receive everything through it and turn back towards God by way of it, Intelligence is also the Gate through which creatures approach God.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01205

This is what the saying of Imam Ja'far means by “a secret that only a secret can teach.” The prophetic Word eternally stands between God and creation as the one that reveals and interprets. Because revelation continually emerges within the primordial Muhammadan Reality, the Imams themselves are “the place of the eternal prophetic message.” At the first maqam, they remain enclosed within the mystery of what has never been revealed. Here, by contrast, they are the place where revelation happens: where its light descends and its stars come to rest.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01206

At the second maqam, they are the inner meaning of the inner. At the third, they are the inner meaning of the outward: the hidden meaning of what the Muhammadan Word reveals. They guard the law brought by the Prophet. They are at once the keepers of the treasure and the treasure itself, the secret that must be passed on and the secret that alone can pass it on to the beings below them.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01207

4. The fourth maqam is identified directly with the Imamate. It is the level of the outward meaning (zahir). This does not mean that the Imamate is merely outward. On the contrary, the eternal Imamate, as understood at the second and third levels, is precisely the secret that hides and remains hidden beneath the outward form of prophetic revelation: the “secret that remains secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01208

The Twelve Imams share a single essence and are “the place of the prophetic message” because the teachings entrusted to God's Messenger are preserved within them. While the outward form of religion governs life, they guard those teachings' hidden meaning.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01209

At this level, then, the Imam is God's guarantor and witness, the one who answers for God before humanity: His Face turned towards the Earth, the eye through which He looks upon human beings. The Imam opens fortified castles and abandoned wells; he offers shelter to those who have been cast out, safety to those who are afraid, and help to believers. He remains God's unseen representative (caliph) in this world throughout the Great Occultation, until the present great age—the present Aeon—reaches its end.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01210
We can now see, with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, that these levels are already summed up in a conversation between the Fourth Imam and Jabir al-Ju'fi, quoted earlier (pp. 121 and following):
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01211

Do you know, Jabir, what gnosis is—what it means to possess true spiritual knowledge (ma'rifa)? It is: (1) the fulfilment of tawhid, affirming God's oneness at the level where we can speak of God only by denying all comparisons; (2) knowledge of the ma'ani, the divine qualities and positive meanings that human beings can understand; (3) knowledge of the “Gates” (abwab), the thresholds where the prophetic mission of each prophet comes into view; (4) knowledge of the Imam; (5) knowledge of the “Pillars,” the four immortal Living Ones; (6) knowledge of the Nuqaba; and (7) knowledge of the Nujaba.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01212

We have already seen that the last two groups are the spiritual “chiefs” and “nobles” who form a hidden hierarchy, with the Imam at its centre or pole (Qutb). In the present age, when religion's outward form prevails and the Imam is hidden from public sight, these figures too remain concealed.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01213

We must recognise that they exist, but we cannot point them out or identify them by name. Their names belong to the Imam's secret. The first three points in the saying correspond, one by one, to the first three maqams we have just described. Points four through seven together belong to the fourth.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01214

We have had to compress a great deal into this brief explanation of the four maqams described in the two versions of Imam Ja'far's saying. Even so, what we have seen should help us understand his allusions. The prophetic Word appears through a succession of levels, each one a further descent or manifestation (tanazzulat) of revelation. At every level, the revelation has a special dwelling place, a secret preserved at its heart: the Imamate of the Twelve Imams, which is the inner meaning of revelation at every stage.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01215

From this idea grow the general Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams (see Chapter VI below). It also opens up the many levels of spiritual interpretation discussed earlier: the different depths at which we can discover the outward and inner meanings of the Qur'an. Each level at which the prophetic Word is revealed is also a new manifestation of the eternal Qur'an as it descends from the original pattern of the Book (Umm al-Kitab), beginning at the level of “the secret still wrapped in secret.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
en-book-1-ch-5-s2
2. The Descent of the Sacred Book Through the Levels of Reality
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01216

How is the eternal divine Word related to the Book that gives that Word a material form in the world we experience ('alam al-shahada)? This is one of the central questions facing any philosophy of prophecy that grows out of a religion founded on revelation. Mulla Sadra Shirazi sums up that approach particularly well:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01217

The Word that comes down from God is Word in one sense and Book in another. Because the Word belongs to the world of the divine Command ('alam al-amr), it differs from the Book, which belongs to the world of created things [...].
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01218

Since the Word belongs to the world of the Command, its dwelling place is in people's hearts: “It is in the hearts of believers, and only those who have been given knowledge can perceive it” (Qur'an 29:48), and “only those who know can understand it” (29:42). The Book, by contrast, belongs to the created world ('alam al-khalq). Its dwelling place is in written tablets that have a physical form and can be seen by anyone—for example, the tablets of Moses.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01219

But as for the Word, “none may touch it except the Pure Ones” (56:78). It is a “sublime Qur'an” (56:76), of exalted rank, upon a “secret tablet” (Tabula secreta; the Preserved Tablet, Lawh mahfuz, 85:22), “which none may touch except the Pure Ones, a revelation from the Lord of the worlds” (56:78–79).
